1142.title: Imagine the scene
1142.hook: Ignatius asks you to enter a gospel story with all your senses
1142.howItsDone: In Ignatian prayer, people often read a short gospel passage, picture the place, enter the scene with their senses, and then speak with Jesus about what stirred; retreat guides and spiritual directors often lead this.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first week: honest sorrow, held by a mercy that came first. Your line was loved, as I am.

Dust on the road out of Jericho. A crowd moving, loud, pushing. At the edge of the road sits a blind beggar named Bartimaeus, first met on day two hundred five. He hears that Jesus of Nazareth is passing, and he starts shouting. People tell him to be quiet. He shouts louder. Jesus stops. Mark tells it in a handful of lines. Ignatius of Loyola would slow it right down. He'd ask you to stand on that road. Feel the grit. Hear the crowd. Watch the beggar throw off his cloak and jump up. The practice's name is the instruction: imagine the scene.
screen: `A BLIND MAN ON THE JERICHO ROAD.`
`THE CROWD SAYS HUSH. HE SHOUTS LOUDER.`

segments.voice: In the Exercises, Ignatius opens many prayer times with what he calls a composition of place: seeing the spot where the story happens. For the birth of Jesus, he suggests picturing the road from Nazareth to Bethlehem: how long, how wide, flat or through valleys. He isn't after a history lesson. He's after presence. Later in the day, he suggests going back over the same scene one sense at a time: what you'd see and hear, even what you'd smell and taste and touch. This second move is known as the application of the senses. Why bother? A story read from a distance stays on the page. A story you stand inside starts asking you things. On the Jericho road, Jesus asks a strange question, when anyone can see what the man needs: "What wilt thou that I should do unto thee?" Bartimaeus answers: "Lord, that I might receive my sight." Standing on the road, the question can turn and land on the one praying. What do you want? Ignatius trusted that God could work through the imagination, and he didn't treat it as making things up. The imagined details may not match the real road, and that's all right. The gospel text stays the anchor; the imagined scene is a way of paying close attention to it. For some, pictures come easily. Others mostly hear, or only sense the mood. Some teachers of this prayer say one sense is enough to begin.
screen: `WHAT WILT THOU THAT I SHOULD DO UNTO THEE?`

segments.voice: Choose the Jericho road, or any gospel story you know, and see the place first: the ground under your feet, the light, how far off Jesus is. Then go sense by sense, the crowd's noise, the dust, the warmth, and find where you're standing, in the crowd or by the road. Let the question reach you, what do you want, and if you pray, answer him; if not, just notice what answer comes.
Imagine the scene. Ignatius' way into a gospel story: see the place, use each sense, and let the story speak back.
Your line: step into the story. The gospel text stays the anchor. Until tomorrow.

1143.title: The call of the king
1143.hook: the second week: Christ calls, and you ask to follow closely
1143.howItsDone: In the Spiritual Exercises, the meditation on the call of the king opens the second week; retreatants then pray through gospel scenes of Jesus' life, asking to know, love and follow him more closely.

segments.voice: Yesterday, imagine the scene: Ignatius put you on the Jericho road. Your line was step into the story.

A king stands before his people and makes an offer. He's setting out on a hard campaign. Whoever comes with him will eat what he eats and wear what he wears, work beside him by day and keep watch with him by night. They'll share the hardship, then the victory. Ignatius of Loyola sets that scene at the start of the second week of his Spiritual Exercises. He asks the one praying to picture a good leader calling like that, and what a decent person would answer. Then he turns the picture around. If that's how people answer an earthly king, what about Christ?

In the Gospels, a call can be very short. Jesus walks by the Sea of Galilee, sees Simon and Andrew casting a net, and says: "Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men." Then: "And they straightway left their nets, and followed him." No speech, no terms. Ignatius slows that moment down. In his meditation, Christ the king calls the whole world, and each person one by one, to share his work and his hardship, so as to share his glory. Anyone with judgment, Ignatius says, would offer themselves for the work. But some will want to offer more: to follow Christ even in bearing wrongs and in poverty, if that's where he leads. That bigger answer isn't a boast. It's a request. From here on, the grace Ignatius has people ask for runs close to this: to know Jesus more from the inside, to love him more, and to follow him more closely. Know, love, follow, in that order. It's hard to follow someone you've only heard about, so next come gospel stories: the birth, the hidden years, the baptism, the calls by the lake. The one praying watches Jesus up close before deciding anything. An old English prayer, which tradition gives to Richard of Chichester, asks to see him more clearly, love him more dearly, and follow him more nearly. Today's line borrows its end. Following more nearly isn't a leap into heroics. It's one step closer than yesterday.

Stand by the lake, a wet net in your hands, and hear the call, short and plain. Notice what rises, eagerness, hesitation, a list of reasons this isn't a good time, and don't fix any of it. If you pray, ask in your own words to know him more, love him more, and follow him more nearly; if you don't, notice one thing you'd want to move a step closer to.
The call of the king. Ignatius' meditation that opens the second week: Christ calls each person to share his work, and the generous answer asks to follow him more closely.

1144.title: Two standards
1144.hook: two banners: riches, honor, pride, or poverty, insults, humility
1144.howItsDone: In the Spiritual Exercises, the Two Standards is prayed during the second week and is followed by a colloquy asking to be received under Christ's standard.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the call of the king: know him, love him, follow him. Your line was to follow more nearly.

Two camps on two great fields. Near Babylon, a banner held by the enemy of human nature, who sits on a throne of fire and smoke. Near Jerusalem, Christ's banner, and Christ stands in a lowly place. That's the stage Ignatius of Loyola sets in the second week of his Spiritual Exercises. An old word for a banner carried into battle is a standard, so the meditation is called the two standards. But Ignatius isn't painting a war movie. He's drawing a map of how a life slides, one small step at a time, toward one banner or the other.
screen: `A MAP OF HOW A LIFE SLIDES.`

segments.voice: Under the first banner, Ignatius says, the tempter works in three steps. First, riches: the urge to have. Then honor: the wish to be admired for what you have. Then pride: the swollen sense of being above others. From those three, he says, the tempter leads on to all the other vices. The first step doesn't look wicked. Wanting things is ordinary. It's the ladder that worries him. Under the second banner, Christ sends his friends out with a plan that mirrors it. First, poverty: at the very least poverty of spirit, a loose grip on things, and actual poverty if God calls someone there. Then a willingness to be overlooked, even insulted, instead of praised. Then humility. Three steps against three. Jesus puts the choice plainly in Matthew: "No man can serve two masters." And Paul traces the second path in Christ himself, who "made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant." No reputation: the second step, lived by the one who carries the banner. This meditation can be misheard as a call to be miserable, or to go looking for insults. Ignatius is careful. The one praying asks to be received under Christ's banner, and to be given these things only if they serve God. It's a check on direction, not a hunt for hardship. And it's honest about how pride usually gets in: not with a crash, but through a small, reasonable-looking first step.

See the two fields and the two banners lifting in the wind, then think back over the last day or two: where did you reach for more, want to be seen or praised, or slide toward feeling above someone, and where did you let go, let someone else have the credit, or take the lower seat? Don't judge it; just see which way you leaned. If you pray, you can ask to stand under Christ's banner.
Two standards. Ignatius' meditation on two banners: riches, honor and pride under one; poverty, insults and humility under the other.
Your line: under his banner. A loose grip, a lower seat, and no hunt for hardship. Until tomorrow.

1145.title: The third and fourth weeks
1145.hook: walking with Christ through the passion, then the joy of resurrection
1145.howItsDone: In the Spiritual Exercises, the third week contemplates Christ's passion, from the Last Supper to the tomb, and the fourth week his resurrection appearances, ending with the Contemplation to Attain Love.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two standards: two banners, two ladders. Your line was under his banner.

"Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep." Paul wrote that to the Christians in Rome, about how to treat one another. The last two weeks of Ignatius of Loyola's Spiritual Exercises ask for something close to it, with one friend at the center. In the third week, the one praying walks with Jesus through his passion: the supper, the garden, the trial, the cross, the tomb. In the fourth week, through the resurrection and the days after. Two very different weeks, and one request running through both: to be with him in whatever he's going through.

In the third week, Ignatius asks for a grace that can surprise people. Not to explain the cross. Not even, first of all, to feel guilty. He asks for sorrow with Christ in sorrow: grief, tears, an inner pain at the pain Christ bears for the one praying. It's the prayer of someone sitting beside a friend in a hospital room. He even suggests noticing how, in the passion, the divinity seems to hide itself and lets the human Jesus suffer terribly. So the one praying stays near and keeps watch, the way Jesus asked his friends to watch with him in the garden. In the fourth week, the grace turns over: to be glad and rejoice because of the glory and joy of Christ risen. John gives that moment one plain sentence: "Then were the disciples glad, when they saw the Lord." Ignatius also asks the one praying to watch how the risen Christ consoles his friends, the way one friend comforts another. Here's what makes these weeks hard. Sorrow and joy on someone else's behalf both mean stepping out of your own center. The fourth week's joy isn't about your own good news. It's gladness that things have gone well for him. That's an ordinary human skill too, and a tricky one. Crying at a sad film can come easier than being really glad when a friend gets the thing you wanted. The church calendar keeps both in one shape: Good Friday, and then Easter.

First stay a while near the cross, or near someone you know who is suffering right now, without trying to fix anything. Then turn: go to the garden on the first morning, or bring to mind someone whose life just went well, and let any gladness be for them, not for you. If you pray, hold both before God; if not, notice how each one sits in your body.
The third and fourth weeks. The passion, then the resurrection, prayed as a friend: sorrow with Christ in sorrow, and joy with Christ in joy.

1146.title: Consolation and desolation
1146.hook: moods that draw you toward or away from God
1146.howItsDone: In Ignatian spirituality, people notice consolation and desolation in the daily examen and talk them over with a spiritual director, who helps them read which way the movements are pulling.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sorrow and then joy, both on his behalf. Your line was with him in both.

Here's a question for any ordinary afternoon: which way am I drifting? Not how am I doing. Which way. Back on day one hundred six, a dry prayer still counted. Ignatius goes further, with rules for noticing movements inside a person. His account traces them to the sickbed from a week ago: the shattered leg, the reading, the daydreams. Some daydreams left him dry and restless. Others left him content and drawn toward God. So he watched the aftertaste. His name for the second pull is today's word: consolation.

Consolation, for Ignatius, is any movement inside that draws a person toward God: being set on fire with love of God, tears that move toward love, any growth in faith, hope and love, an inner joy and quiet that pulls toward heavenly things. Desolation is the opposite pull: darkness, restlessness, a tug toward low things, feeling without hope or love, lazy, lukewarm, sad, as if cut off from God. Here's the surprise. Consolation isn't the same as feeling good, and desolation isn't the same as feeling bad. Ignatius counts tears of grief over one's sins as consolation, because they draw toward God. And a cheerful, busy week can be desolation underneath, if it's quietly drifting away. The test is direction, not temperature. Paul's list works like a compass: "But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith." When those grow, something's moving the right way. Ignatius adds a subtler detail. The same feeling can mean different things depending on where a person is heading. For someone sliding toward harm, a nagging unease can be a mercy, a knock on the door. For someone trying to grow toward God, a voice saying what's the point can be the pull away. So he asks people to notice the arrow under the mood. And desolation isn't automatically a verdict. Ignatius gives three reasons it comes: sometimes our own slackness, sometimes a testing, sometimes to show that consolation is a gift, not an achievement. It's weather to read, not a sentence passed. And if what's the point ever turns into thoughts of ending your life, please reach out: call or text 988 in the US, or local emergency help.

Run back over the day like a short film, watching for direction, not good or bad moments. Where did something open you up, toward people, toward God, if that's your language, and where did something close you down or make everything feel pointless? Name one of each, and if you pray, thank God for the first and bring him the second.
Consolation. Ignatius' word for any movement inside that draws a person toward God, and toward faith, hope and love, even when it comes with tears.
Your line: which way am I drifting? The arrow matters more than the mood. See you tomorrow.

1147.title: Rules for discernment
1147.hook: in desolation, don't make big changes
1147.howItsDone: Ignatian retreat guides and spiritual directors teach the rules for discernment of spirits, and people use them when weighing decisions, often waiting to choose until desolation has passed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, consolation and desolation: the arrow under the mood. Your line was which way am I drifting?

It's late, the house is quiet, and everything feels wrong. The job seems pointless. The friendship seems over. Faith feels hollow. And in that mood a decision shows up, looking very clear: quit, send the message, walk away. In the morning, with coffee and some light through the window, the same choice can look very different. Ignatius of Loyola wrote a rule for exactly that night, short enough to remember half asleep, and it comes out of yesterday's two words. Today: rules for discernment.

Discernment means sorting: telling one thing from another. Back on day six hundred eighty-eight, the first letter of John put it this way: "Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God." Try them. Test them. Ignatius' rules are a field guide for that testing, and today rests on the fifth. In time of desolation, he says, never make a change. Stay firm in what you decided before the darkness came, in the calm or in consolation. His reason is plain. In desolation, the voice giving advice isn't a good counselor, and a decision made in that fog tends to follow the fog. But he doesn't say do nothing. His next rule says push back against the desolation itself: pray a little more, think it through, look honestly at what's happening, do some small thing against the mood. Change your effort, not your plans. For the bright days he says: in consolation, think ahead to how you'll be when it passes, and store up strength for then. And stay humble, remembering how little you could manage in the low times. He also pictures temptation as a commander who studies a fortress and attacks where the wall is weakest. Each person's weak place is different, and knowing your own is part of keeping watch. None of this means desolation is failure, or that every hard feeling is an enemy. It means some choices deserve daylight, the big ones especially: the job, the move, the vow. And if the dark ever brings thoughts of harming yourself, that isn't a choice to shelve: call or text 988 in the US, or local emergency help, right away.

Ask whether there's a choice you've been tempted to make in a low or rattled moment: a message to send, something to quit, a purchase, a door to slam. Don't decide anything now; set it down gently on a shelf for a calmer day, and notice what it's like to leave it there. If you pray, you can bring it to God and ask for light.
Discernment. Sorting the movements inside, testing which pull is which, and choosing in the light.
Your line: never decide in the dark. Morning light can change the whole picture. Until tomorrow.

1148.title: Take, Lord, receive
1148.hook: Ignatius' prayer offering liberty, memory, understanding and will
1148.carry: your love and grace are enough
1148.howItsDone: The Suscipe comes at the end of the Spiritual Exercises, in the Contemplation to Attain Love; Jesuits and others shaped by Ignatian spirituality pray it on retreat and in daily prayer, and it has been set to music as a hymn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rules for discernment: in desolation, make no change. Your line was never decide in the dark.

The Spiritual Exercises end with an inventory. After praying through the life of Jesus, start to finish, Ignatius of Loyola asks the one praying to count up gifts: being made at all, being redeemed, and everything particular to their own life. Then he asks a question that sounds simple and isn't: given all that, what would you give back? His answer is a short prayer, known by its first word in Latin. Suscipe. Receive. It's today's word, and it closes this stretch with Ignatius.

Ignatius opens this last contemplation with two short notes about love. First, love shows itself more in deeds than in words. Second, love is a sharing: the one who loves gives what they have to the beloved, and the beloved gives back. Then comes the prayer. In plain English, it runs like this. Take, Lord, and receive all my liberty, my memory, my understanding, and my whole will, all that I have and possess. You gave it to me; to you, Lord, I return it. All of it is yours; do with it what you will. Give me your love and your grace; that is enough for me. Look at what's offered. Not money, not achievements. Freedom, memory, understanding, will: the inside of a person. And look at the reason. Paul asks the church at Corinth: "what hast thou that thou didst not receive?" Nothing is handed over that wasn't a gift first. The request at the end is small on purpose: love and grace. Paul hears something like it from Christ: "My grace is sufficient for thee." That's where this week has been heading: a gospel scene stepped into, the king's call, two banners, the watch at the cross and the empty tomb, reading the drift inside, and not deciding in the dark. It all ends not with a technique, but with a gift handed back. This is a hard prayer to mean all the way through. Some teachers of the Exercises call it a prayer to grow into, not a test to pass.
screen: `WHAT HAST THOU THAT THOU DIDST NOT RECEIVE?`
`A WEEK THAT ENDS WITH A GIFT RETURNED.`

segments.voice: Go slowly through the four, pausing on each: liberty, the freedom you have today; memory, what you carry; understanding, how you make sense of things; will, what you choose. If you pray, say Ignatius' prayer phrase by phrase, offering each one back; if you don't, simply hold each gift for a moment and notice where it came from.
Suscipe. Latin for receive: the first word of Ignatius' prayer offering liberty, memory, understanding and will, and asking only for love and grace.
Your line: your love and grace are enough. Everything offered was a gift first. Rest well.
